# ToolingSetup

**Class** · namespace `VRFramework.Core.Editors.Setup` · assembly `VRFramework.Core.Editors` · [view source](https://git.cie-group.cz/vr-framework/vrf4/core/-/blob/main/Editor/Setup/ToolingSetup.cs#L32)

The half of the setup that is about the machine rather than the project: the agent tooling the
framework ships a window for, and the editor layout that arranges those windows.

A project configured for VR still is not a project anyone can work in. The framework's
OpenCode window needs an opencode binary, opencode needs to know about Unity's MCP relay
before it can see the editor at all, and the relay only exists once something copies it out
of the AI Assistant package. Each of those was a page of setup instructions nobody read;
they are steps now.

Everything here is written to be safe to run twice and to report rather than throw: none of
it is needed to build the project, so a machine that refuses to install a tool should end
up with a configured project and one line in the report, not a failed setup.

## Methods

### ApplyEditorLayout() {#applyeditorlayout}

Arranges the editor the way the framework's windows expect, as the last thing the setup
does. It has to be last: loading a layout closes every window, including the one reporting
on the setup, so the setup window is opened again on the other side - the run's record
outlives the window and comes straight back with it.

```csharp
public static void ApplyEditorLayout()
```

### ConfigureOpenCode() {#configureopencode}

Writes the two things opencode cannot work out for itself into the developer's own config:
where Unity's MCP relay is, and what the free DeepSeek model's real limits are.

This is the user's file rather than the project's, because both facts are about this
machine and this account: the relay lives under the home directory, and the model limit
is a property of the provider, not of the project. The file is merged rather than
written, and a copy of the old one is kept beside it.

```csharp
public static void ConfigureOpenCode()
```

### EnableUnityMcpBridge() {#enableunitymcpbridge}

Turns the editor's MCP bridge on, which is the half of the connection that lives inside
Unity. Reached by reflection on purpose: the framework must still compile in a project that
does not have the AI Assistant package.

### InstallOpenCode() {#installopencode}

Installs opencode with the installer its authors publish, unless it is already on this
machine. The install is a download and a shell, so it gets its own step and its own clock
rather than blocking the editor.

```csharp
public static void InstallOpenCode()
```

### InstallUnityMcpRelay() {#installunitymcprelay}

Copies the MCP relay out of the AI Assistant package into `~/.unity/relay`, which is
the stable path every MCP client config points at. Unity's own settings page does this the
first time somebody opens it; doing it here means the config written by the next step
points at something that exists.

```csharp
public static void InstallUnityMcpRelay()
```

### OpenCodeInstalled() {#opencodeinstalled}

Polled by the runner until the installer is done, then reads the result off disk.
A script reload throws the process handle away without stopping the process, so when the
handle is gone the recorded id is asked instead of assuming the work is over.
